_comment: The MOC copilot agents the platform serves, and the single source of truth for
provisioning their LiteLLM virtual keys.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL
Aurora is created and destroyed with the cluster, so the virtual keys do not survive
the evening. That trade is only acceptable because recreating them is one command
reading one file -- bench/scripts/provision_keys.py -- rather than an afternoon of
reissuing credentials by hand. Without this list, session-scoped Aurora would be a
false economy.
THE NAMES ARE PLACEHOLDERS AND SHOULD BE CONFIRMED
The brief says 'at least 7 MOC agents' and deliberately does not name them. These
seven are derived from the document categories that actually exist in the retrieval
corpus -- metric-catalog, data-dictionary, analysis-playbook, data-governance,
service-catalog, knowledge-base, daily-operations -- so each has real material to
answer from rather than being invented wholesale. Ask the mentor for the real roster
before quoting per-agent numbers in the report.
ACCESS LEVEL IS NOT YET ENFORCED PER AGENT. The guardrail pins access_level to the
deployment default and never reads it from the request, because reading it from a
client-supplied field is privilege escalation. Mapping an authenticated virtual key to
the level below is the work docs/litellm-aurora-implementation.md calls out as still
needed before production. The values here describe the intent, not current behaviour.
budget_usd is a monthly ceiling per agent. They sum to less than the project budget on
purpose: one agent looping must not be able to spend everything. NOTE that this is
currently decorative: LiteLLM derives spend from its model-pricing map, and the chart
configures no input_cost_per_token/output_cost_per_token for the self-hosted models, so
accounted spend stays at zero and no budget can ever trip. Setting those two values is
the same work that makes TC2 computable inside LiteLLM instead of in a spreadsheet.
moc-da-pilot IS NOT AN AGENT, and it is the one entry here that serves humans.
It is the key the chat UI holds server-side for the GreenSM data analyst pilot, so that
the analysts never handle a credential and a nightly Aurora teardown costs them nothing
-- only the UI's config is refreshed. Pinned to the 7B model alone: the 1.5B needs
decode-time citation forcing to stay grounded, which is an acceptable trade for an
automated agent and not for a colleague reading the answer as advice.
It is also NOT what TC4 counts. TC4's '>=5 DA' is five digital agents, already met by
the seven above; the analysts in this pilot are the real-project integration goal, a
separate thing. Per-person attribution for them lives in the UI's own logs, not in the
end_user Prometheus label, which stays one series for the whole UI.
THE ROSTER IS NOW THE ONE FROM THE BRIEF, NOT ONE WE INVENTED.
The brief names this platform 'nen tang cho DA#19/#20/#32/#39/#41/#44/#45', so TC4's
'>=5 DA chay tren nen tang' means at least five of THOSE project teams actually calling
it. The seven ids here are those projects. The earlier ids -- moc-analytics, moc-datadict
and so on -- were placeholders derived from corpus categories, and reporting per-agent
numbers under them would have described a roster that does not exist.
description and corpus_focus are deliberately left UNCONFIRMED rather than guessed. We do
not know what DA#32 does, and a plausible-sounding guess here would propagate into the
dashboard, the report and the acceptance review as though it were fact. Fill each one in
from its own team, not from imagination.
models lists both tiers for every project for the same reason: tier choice depends on the
workload, and nobody has told us theirs yet. See the model-tier note -- 7B for the hard
work, 1.5B for the simple, and never the same workload sent to both. Narrow each entry
once its team says what it is doing.
AND TC4 IS NOT A TECHNICAL TASK. Minting keys does not satisfy it; five other teams
choosing to integrate does. That has a lead time nobody here controls, so it starts now.
clients/python/ exists to make saying yes cheap for them.
